comment.value:
This paper introduces ClinicalLab, a suite for aligning LLM-based medical agents with real-world diagnostics. ClinicalLab includes ClinicalBench, a benchmark of 1500 real cases across 24 departments and 150 diseases, and ClinicalMetrics, four evaluation metrics. The authors propose ClinicalAgent, showing improved robustness and alignment with clinical diagnostic workflows.

Strengths:
- Reviewers noted ClinicalBench as a major contribution. It is rigorously developed from real hospital records, resulting in a benchmark that reflects realistic diagnostic complexity rather than synthetic or MCQ-style tasks.
- The paper conducts a comprehensive evaluation of diverse LLMs (17 general purpose and medical domain LLMs), while showing ClinicalAgent outperforming single models to demonstrate the importance of aligning AI workflows with real clinical specialization.
- Offering the dataset in both Chinese and English enables wider adoption of the dataset by the global research community.

Weaknesses:

Most of the concerns raised by the reviewers were resolved during the discussion period such as the need for dataset transparency (the originating hospital), more LLMs to be included in the experiments, providing compute cost and experiment details for better reproducibility. Two concerns were the crux of the discussion:
- Ethical concerns were raised regarding the use of real-world medical records. The authors promised to provide necessary documents.
- More importantly, the initial metrics proposed by the authors were not able to measure the end-to-end model performance as opposed to the authors’ claim. However, the authors adopted suggestions from the reviewers during the rebuttal, and proposed an improved metric, which is promised to be reflected in the final version.

author_final_remarks.value:
We sincerely appreciate the efforts of the AC and reviewers during the rebuttal period. In response to the main concerns raised by the reviewers, we have provided the following clarifications and additional analyses:

* **Evaluation protocol** We explicitly separate *single-point* (gold inputs per stage; upper bounds) and *end-to-end* (each stage consumes prior outputs; captures error propagation). We added **end-to-end evaluations for baseline LLMs** and made this distinction prominent in the paper.

* **Primary holistic metric.** We introduce **Cumulative Diagnostic Accuracy (CDA)** as the main end-to-end metric. Results quantify error accumulation and show **ClinicalAgent** remains more robust than strong single models. Besides, we will also report micro-averaged accuracy, plus paired t-tests and confidence intervals to provide significance and variance.

* **Ethics & provenance.** We now clearly state the dataset source (24 departments; 12 physicians; title distribution provided). Demographics for **N=1,500** are reported (sex and age buckets). Ethics approval letters (Chinese + notarized English), licenses, Dataset Card, de-identification pipeline, and access controls are included.

* **Model coverage & comparisons**
  We include recent strong baselines (e.g., Claude-4, O3) and, in the revision, add clearer **within-/cross-family** comparisons to yield actionable design insights.

* **Scope & limitations.** We state adherence to **mainland China clinical guidelines**; English samples are **machine-translated**. Imaging tasks use expert text reports(for LLMs); we note this scope and its implications.


----

We also want to highlight the contributions of this work as follows:

* **ClinicalBench.** The first real-case-based, leakage-controlled, *end-to-end*, multi-department benchmark for clinical diagnosis with LLMs, covering **24 departments** and **150 diseases** (1,500 cases).

* **ClinicalMetrics.** Four task-aligned metrics for practicality and effectiveness in clinical settings; now complemented by **CDA** as the primary holistic end-to-end indicator and **micro-averaged accuracy**.

* **ClinicalAgent.** An agent aligned with modern clinical workflows that **outperforms competitive single LLMs** under **CDA** and exhibits greater robustness to error propagation across the diagnostic chain.

Again, we deeply appreciate the hard work of the AC and reviewers and generous service. Please accept our highest respect and gratitude!

Dear Reviewer,

Thanks for your further clarification and valuable suggestions, which have been very helpful in improving this work. We have carefully addressed each of the issues raised and added new experimental results, as presented below.

Q1:  A critical analysis is missing, such as an investigation into how a high-performing LLM's performance degrades when it is shifted from isolated tasks to a sequential pipeline.

A1: We consider the two scenarios you mentioned as follows:

1. **Single-point evaluation**: Each stage receives gold-standard inputs, allowing us to measure its solvability and establish the theoretical upper bound of performance in isolation.
2. **End-to-end evaluation**: Beginning from triage, each subsequent stage consumes the output from the previous stage, faithfully simulating the real clinical workflow and enabling direct measurement of error accumulation across the diagnostic chain.

In the original manuscript:

* **Table 2** (LLM performance) adopted *single-point evaluation*.
* **Table 4** (three ClinicalAgent settings) adopted *end-to-end evaluation*, and the appendix case studies also followed this paradigm.
* We did not perform single-point evaluation for ClinicalAgent, since the system is intended to operate *autonomously*, and in real-world diagnosis, gold-standard intermediate inputs are unavailable.

Following your suggestion, we have added *end-to-end* evaluations for the baseline LLMs. The results are shown below:

| Model    | Mode       | Acc  | DIFR | PD   | DB   | DD   | FD   | PT   | TP   | Imaging Diag. | DWR  | CDR  | Accept. | Avg  |
| -------- | ---------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ------------- | ---- | ---- | ------- | ---- |
| Claude-4 | Single     | 72.9 | 98.3 | 79.4 | 52.3 | 39.1 | 57.1 | 53.1 | 40.5 | 47.1          | 15.6 | 39.1 | 14.9    | 59.9 |
| Claude-4 | End-to-end | 72.9 | 98.3 | 79.0 | 50.2 | 33.1 | 52.9 | 39.8 | 33.1 | 40.8          | 15.1 | 33.9 | 13.3    | 55.6 |
| O3       | Single     | 75.1 | 99.2 | 86.9 | 51.2 | 43.8 | 59.4 | 52.7 | 41.3 | 50.2          | 17.1 | 42.5 | 16.3    | 62.2 |
| O3       | End-to-end | 75.8 | 99.2 | 80.0 | 49.3 | 39.6 | 55.2 | 46.8 | 37.6 | 51.3          | 15.7 | 37.9 | 15.1    | 59.4 |

---

**Result Analysis**

Comparing *single-point* and *end-to-end* modes reveals a consistent performance drop across most stages for both baseline models. This confirms the expected **error accumulation** effect when outputs from earlier stages propagate downstream.

* For **Claude-4**, the average score declines from **59.9** to **55.6** (−4.3 points). The largest stage-level degradation occurs in TP and DD, reflecting the compounding impact of upstream diagnostic inaccuracies.
* For **O3**, the average score decreases from **62.2** to **59.4** (−2.8 points). While the drop is smaller than Claude-4’s, the same vulnerable stages are observed, indicating that this phenomenon is model-agnostic.

These findings establish a quantitative baseline for error propagation in multi-stage clinical pipelines, providing a clear reference point for evaluating improvements from ClinicalAgent or other sequential reasoning systems.

---

Q2: A holistic metric that reflects the outcome of this sequential process is required.

A2: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. Reviewer J4MA previously raised a similar point, which led us to propose a dedicated solution and compute the corresponding results, as detailed below.

To capture an overall measure that reflects the success of the entire uninterrupted process, we introduce the **Cumulative Diagnostic Accuracy (CDA)**. CDA is defined as the probability of reaching a correct final diagnosis when all intermediate stages are executed sequentially without any gold-standard inputs. This metric directly evaluates true end-to-end performance, encompassing all sources of error propagation along the diagnostic pipeline.

Following your advice, we evaluated CDA for O3 and Claude-4 under both single-point and end-to-end settings:

| Model        | Mode       | CDA (%)  |
| ------------ | ---------- | -------- |
| Claude-4     | Single     | **41.6** |
| Claude-4     | End-to-end | **38.6** |
| O3           | Single     | **44.6** |
| O3           | End-to-end | **41.5** |

---

**Result Analysis**

The CDA results clearly demonstrate the performance gap between the theoretical upper bound (*single-point*) and the realistic autonomous execution (*end-to-end*).

* **Claude-4** shows a drop of 3.0 percentage points (41.6 → 38.6),
* **O3** drops by 3.1 points (44.6 → 41.5),

Overall, CDA complements stage-wise metrics by summarizing holistic diagnostic success in a single value. It captures both the solvability of each stage and the robustness of the system to error accumulation.

---

Thank you again for your diligent review and constructive feedback. We have formulated a clear revision plan based on your comments and will reflect all changes in the revised manuscript.

Thanks for acknowledging our clarifications and future plans, this is a great encouragement to the team. In response to your key question: why some intermediate metrics in the “Acc~Imaging Diag.” table score relatively low while the overall average (Avg.) remains high, we provide the following explanation and revisions.

---

### 1. Root cause of the “inflated average”

As described in the caption of Table 2, *Avg.* is the simple arithmetic mean of 8 tasks × 9 metrics. Because DIFR and PD score markedly higher than the other metrics, they exert an “uplift effect” during averaging, masking the difficulties revealed by the more challenging metrics (*DWR*, *CDR*, etc.) and creating the impression of an inflated overall score.

### 2. *Cumulative Diagnostic Accuracy (CDA)* is a more appropriate metric

Per your suggestion, we introduce **CDA** in the revised manuscript. CDA executes all intermediate steps sequentially, without any gold inputs, and records the final diagnostic accuracy. This directly measures end-to-end performance and avoids bias from mixing tasks of different scales.

| Model        | Mode       | CDA (%)  |
| ------------ | ---------- | -------- |
| Claude-4     | Single     | **41.6** |
| Agent #3 @ 1 | Single     | **51.6** |
| Agent #3 @ 1 | End-to-end | **45.5** |

Under the single-step setting, *Agent #3* achieves a CDA of 51.6 %. When run end-to-end, it still outperforms Claude-4 by 3.9 percentage points, indicating that **ClinicalAgent** mitigates error propagation to some extent.

### 3. Revisions to the manuscript

* **Main text:** Added the CDA table and discussion, directly addressing the “low local metrics yet high overall score” issue.
* **Appendix:** Added representative case studies illustrating how early errors can amplify downstream.

---

In summary, the high scores of **DIFR** and **PD** elevate *Avg.*, whereas **CDA** more accurately reflects true end-to-end diagnostic capability in clinical scenarios. We have fully adopted CDA in the revised manuscript and updated the results and conclusions accordingly.
Thanks again for your invaluable suggestions, which have significantly improved our manuscript. If you need any further information, please do not hesitate to let us know.

## Q1. How do you evaluate the performance of the subsequent tasks, using the answers generated by the models or the ground truth answers from previous tasks?

**A1:** We consider the two scenarios you mentioned as two distinct evaluation modes:

1. **Single-point evaluation**: Each stage receives gold-standard inputs to measure its solvability and theoretical upper bound in isolation.

2. **End-to-end evaluation**: Starting from triage, each subsequent stage consumes the model-generated output from the previous stage. This mimics the real clinical workflow and enables direct observation of error propagation along the diagnostic chain.

In the original manuscript:

* **Table 2** (LLM performance) adopts the *single-point evaluation* mode.
* **Table 4** (three ClinicalAgent settings) uses the *end-to-end evaluation* mode; the case studies in the appendix are also based on this approach.
* We did not conduct single-point evaluation on ClinicalAgent, as we expect the system to operate *autonomously*—in real-world diagnostic scenarios, gold-standard intermediate inputs are not available.

---

## Q2. If model-generated answers are fed forward, an early mistake (e.g., at the first task) might cascade and degrade overall performance. Have you quantified this effect? Do you have solutions or insights to mitigate it?

**A2:** Thank you for the insightful question. We have indeed added such analyses. We now report both evaluation modes for the same agent (Agent #3 @ 1) and compare them with Claude-4’s single-point results:

| ------------ | ---------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ------- | ----- | ---- | ---- | ------- | --- |
| Claude-4     | Single     | 72.9 | 98.3 | 79.4 | 52.3 | 39.1 | 57.1 | 53.1 | 40.5 | 47.1    | 15.6  | 39.1 | 14.9 | 59.9    |     |
| Agent #3 @ 1 | Single     | 75.1 | 99.2 | 88.7 | 57.2 | 43.8 | 68.7 | 70.7 | 64.6 | 56.1    | 19.0  | 50.9 | 21.3 | 69.3    |     |
| Agent #3 @ 1 | End-to-end | 75.8 | 99.2 | 84.3 | 50.8 | 39.5 | 60.0 | 56.8 | 43.3 | 49.9    | 17.4  | 43.3 | 17.0 | 62.2    |     |

From single-point to end-to-end, Agent #3 @ 1’s average score drops by 7.1 percentage points. Differential Diagnosis (DD) drops by 4.3 points, and Final Diagnosis (FD) by 8.7 points, confirming that early-stage errors significantly impair downstream reasoning quality. Although Agent #3 @ 1 performs strongly on DIFR, PD, and PT in the single-point setting, it shows clear degradation in DB and DD when evaluated sequentially—highlighting the need for greater robustness to upstream noise.

These findings and analyses will be added to §5.2 of the revised manuscript.

**Mitigation Measures:** We recognize that isolated evaluations of each stage fail to capture the sequential nature of clinical reasoning. To address this, we will introduce *Cumulative Diagnostic Accuracy (CDA)* in the revised version. CDA measures the probability of arriving at the correct final diagnosis when executing all intermediate stages sequentially without gold-standard inputs—directly reflecting true end-to-end performance.

---

## Q3. I am also interested in the performance when using the ground truth answers from previous tasks for each task’s evaluation, which could be regarded as the upper bound.

**A3:** Thank you for your interest. The *single-point mode* results reported in the table in A2 correspond to the upper-bound performance you referred to.

---

Thank you for your detailed rebuttal. I am satisfied with your plan to clarify the distinction between the component-level evaluation and the end-to-end simulation, and to add an absolute metric (i.e., micro-averaged accuracy). 

However, regarding the evaluation framework, my fundamental concerns remain. Your rebuttal regarding the CDR metric focuses on its combination with linguistic quality scores, but this sidesteps my original critique. While I understand the desire to evaluate both decision accuracy and fluency, my original critique was more fundamental: the metric itself is blind to the quality of the intermediate reasoning process. 

For a benchmark to be truly "end-to-end" and for its evaluation to be considered comprehensive, the following analyses are not suggestions, but essential components of a rigorous methodology: 
- (i) A critical analysis is missing, such as an investigation into how a high-performing LLM's performance degrades when it is shifted from isolated tasks to a sequential pipeline. To address this, the paper must include an end-to-end evaluation of the baseline LLMs from Table 2. A direct comparison is necessary, showing a baseline model's performance with ground-truth inputs at each stage versus its performance in a true, self-generated sequential simulation. This experiment is crucial to establishing a clear baseline for error accumulation, independent of your proposed ClinicalAgent method. 
- (ii) Consequently, a holistic metric that reflects the outcome of this sequential process is required. In this respect, I believe the proposed CDR is insufficient. A comprehensive evaluation must feature a primary metric that captures the success of the entire, uninterrupted chain. 

I strongly believe these analyses are fundamental to substantiating the paper's claims about the challenges of end-to-end clinical diagnosis and the effectiveness of the proposed solutions. Likewise, as discussed with Reviewer J4MA, I look forward to seeing these essential analyses (i.e., error accumulation along with proper metrics) performed on at least one or two of the baseline LLMs (and not just on the proposed ClinicalAgent).

We recognize that evaluating each stage in isolation is insufficient to capture the sequential nature of clinical reasoning. To address this, we will introduce **Cumulative Diagnostic Accuracy (CDA)** in the revised version.
CDA: Executes all intermediate stages sequentially without gold inputs and records the probability of a correct final diagnosis, directly assessing truly end-to-end performance.

**Department-level results**: We have already computed every metric for 17 LLMs across 24 departments. Owing to space (≈ 17 × 24 × 8 entries), the full matrix cannot fit in the paper. To serve interested readers, we will publish the complete results on the **ClinicalLab website** and cite the link in the text.

---

Section **§ 3.2** of the manuscript details data cleaning, annotation, and quality control. The full dataset is released in the appendix and supplementary materials and has been downloaded over 200 times, demonstrating its reusability. If you need further clarification on quality control or reproducibility, please let us know and we will respond promptly.
Furthermore, we believe that building a dataset should be a one-time effort, whereas its subsequent use must be fully reproducible. For example, with benchmarks such as GSM8K and HumanEval, we directly use the community-curated versions rather than re-scraping and reconstructing the data each time. Likewise, our Clinical Dataset has been released in a ready-to-use form that supports reproducible reuse.

---

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thorough review of our paper and the valuable feedback and suggestions provided. We are grateful for the reviewer’s recognition of the quality and comprehensiveness of ClinicalLab, the acknowledgment of its value to the research community, and the appreciation of the quality of our paper. Below, we provide detailed responses to all the questions and concerns raised.

**1. Regarding “insufficient comparison with related work” and “no references in Table 1”**
We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out the insufficiencies in our comparison with related work. In the revised version, we will update Table 1 by adding the corresponding references (all of which can currently be found in the “Related Work” section), and we will supplement a systematic comparison with existing methods (e.g., \[1]\[2]\[3]), covering aspects such as the number of models, coverage of clinical tasks, evaluation methods, and metrics. In addition, we will refer to the benchmarking methods summarized in a recent *Nature* review article (\[[https://www.nature.com/articles/s44222-025-00279-5](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44222-025-00279-5)]), and elaborate in the “Related Work” section on the unique contributions of ClinicalAgent compared to existing approaches. Thank you for your valuable suggestion!

**2. Regarding “more LLMs should be included, especially Claude-4, O1, O3, MedGemma, BioMistral”**

We appreciate the reviewer’s comment on the limited coverage of models. In our additional experiments, we have included Claude-4 and O3. Due to time constraints, we have not yet completed evaluations on MedGemma and BioMistral. However, we commit to including the experimental results for these models in a future version and will add them to Table 2 and the Appendix accordingly.

The results for Claude-4 and O3 are as follows:

| Model    | Acc   | DIFR  | PD    | DB    | DD    | FD    | PT    | TP    | Imaging Diagnosis | DWR   | CDR   | Acceptability | Avg   |
| -------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----------------- | ----- | ----- | ------------- | ----- |
| Claude-4 | 72.90 | 98.30 | 79.40 | 52.30 | 39.10 | 57.10 | 53.10 | 40.50 | 47.10             | 15.65 | 39.15 | 14.95         | 59.99 |
| O3       | 75.10 | 99.20 | 86.90 | 51.20 | 43.80 | 59.40 | 52.70 | 41.30 | 50.20             | 17.10 | 42.50 | 16.30         | 62.20 |

As shown, GPT-4o (O3) achieved the best performance on multiple subtasks, with the highest average score (62.20), followed closely by Claude-4 (59.99). Both significantly outperform previous SOTA models such as InternLM2, indicating that the new generation of models has made substantial progress in clinical diagnostic capabilities.

**3. Regarding “Can detailed per-task results for ClinicalAgent be provided?”**

Thank you for your question. We are a bit confused here, as Table 2 presents component-level performance analysis for LLMs, rather than ClinicalAgent’s performance. This is in line with reviewer o4Fw’s endorsement of our “two-stage evaluation framework”: first evaluating the LLM components, and then the end-to-end simulation task with ClinicalAgent. We assume you are suggesting that Table 4 be extended to include fine-grained results for ClinicalAgent across subtasks. If so, we will expand Table 4 in the revised version to include automatic evaluation results for each subtask, and add example outputs in the Appendix to help readers better understand the differences in output quality. This was omitted previously due to space constraints—thank you for the reminder!

**4. Regarding “lack of human expert or traditional ML baseline”**

The ClinicalBench dataset has been carefully annotated and reviewed by medical experts from multiple departments to ensure the professionalism and reliability of the ground truth. Based on this, we established a comprehensive baseline system covering 17 LLMs and three ClinicalAgent variants to evaluate model performance on clinical diagnostic tasks.

ClinicalBench is designed to simulate real clinical diagnostic scenarios, using open-ended QA tasks to avoid the guesswork bias commonly found in multiple-choice datasets. Therefore, introducing a random-guessing baseline is of limited relevance. Moreover, since no single human doctor can realistically cover over 24 departments and more than 150 diseases, using expert ratings as a unified baseline is not feasible. In fact, several recent LLM benchmarks in both medical and cross-domain fields (e.g., \[1–6]) have similarly not included human expert baselines.

In summary, we believe that excluding random guessing and expert baselines is a reasonable and standard choice aligned with current research practices.

**5. Regarding “lack of statistical significance analysis”**

Thank you for the valuable suggestion. We are very willing to include statistical significance analysis in the revised version, but could you please provide more detailed guidance? For example, would you prefer that we use paired t-tests to compare model differences in subtask scores? We will follow your guidance to strengthen the rigor of our experimental analysis.

**6. Regarding “evaluation metric system needs improvement; new metrics not validated”**

Thank you for your attention to our proposed DWR/CDR/DIFR metrics. We respectfully express a differing opinion: these metrics were co-designed with clinical doctors to capture key decision points in the diagnostic process. We provided relevant experimental results in Section 5.2 and Table 4. As shown in Table 4, the weighted sum of these automatic metrics has a strong positive correlation with human scores (Pearson r = 0.811, p = 0.027), indicating that these metrics can serve as reliable surrogates for human evaluation.

As for hallucination detection and safety evaluation, we agree that they are important, but given their complexity and the fact that they go beyond the scope of this study, we regard them as important directions for future work.

**7. Regarding “lack of ablation on model size, architecture, training data”**

Thank you for the suggestion. Our original intent was to horizontally compare the performance of different LLMs on the same tasks. We have already included results for GPT-3.5, GPT-4, and O3, but due to their closed-source nature, it is difficult to conduct ablation experiments on scale and architecture. We plan to add results for the Qwen2.5 series (3B/7B/32B) and its MoE variants in future versions and will perform systematic comparisons under the same task settings. Relevant discussions will be added to Section 6 of the paper.

**8. Regarding “image tasks did not use raw images, bypassing the visual component of VLMs”**

We understand your concern. However, the core goal of this study is to evaluate the clinical performance of large language models (LLMs) and their agent-driven systems, rather than visual-language models (VLMs). Processing raw medical images is a specialized field within medical image analysis and is commonly addressed in conferences such as CVPR and MICCAI.

In ClinicalBench, we invited multiple experts to write high-quality image descriptions using professional terminology to ensure inclusion of all key information. This approach currently offers higher feasibility and consistency. Moreover, as shown in Table 1, existing benchmark datasets also do not mix raw image data with natural language data, highlighting the fundamental differences in task design between the two.

**9. Regarding “lack of details on human evaluation”**

Thank you for the reminder. In the revised manuscript, we will include complete details of human evaluation, including the clinical backgrounds of the seven participating doctors, the number of tasks each was responsible for, a description of the scoring protocol, and the inter-annotator agreement (Cohen’s Kappa ≈ 0.82, indicating strong consistency). Additionally, we will provide the evaluation template and example questionnaire in Appendix A4 to enhance the transparency of the evaluation process.

**10. Regarding “lack of cost and latency analysis”**

We have conducted a preliminary assessment of the invocation cost and response latency for the GPT-4-based ClinicalAgent system. Results show that the average cost per consultation round is approximately \$0.35, with a response latency of about 20.8 seconds. In comparison, the average cost for a single-model baseline is around \$0.12. We will include a comprehensive comparison table in the appendix of the revised manuscript, covering the cost and latency for different models and tasks to better inform practical deployment.

**11. Regarding “more information on hospitals needed”**

11.1 Due to the involvement of real patient data, the hospital ethics committee explicitly requires us not to disclose the names of hospitals, departments, titles, or the exact number of physicians, in order to prevent potential privacy breaches. We have provided compliant descriptions of data sources and participating institutions in Section 3.1 and Appendices A6/A7.

11.2 Information regarding informed consent and ethical approvals has been included in the supplementary materials for the reviewers’ reference.


We genuinely appreciate the diligent and professional nature of your review. Your insightful comments have been invaluable in refining our paper, and we trust that the clarifications offered above adequately address your concerns. We eagerly await your response to our updated submission and thank you once more for your considerable time and effort.

Below, we provide detailed responses to all the questions and concerns raised.

1. Thank you for raising this valuable point. We understand your concerns regarding the DWR as a relative metric. However, we believe that this relativity is not a flaw in DWR; rather, it is a crucial advantage that allows for timely evaluation of model performance in the dynamic environment of rapidly evolving LLMs. In addition, relative metrics are widely used within the community.[1-2]

The original design intent of DWR was to dynamically reflect the relative performance among various models. It is this method of relative evaluation that enables us to effectively differentiate the strengths and weaknesses of models across various departments, despite increasing model diversity and complexity.

In fact, its applicability and subsequent maintenance are closely linked. To address potential issues with the relative metric, we have taken two key actions to resolve them. Firstly, we have made public the average metric scores of each model across different departments, allowing users to quickly calculate the DWR using these results and the code we provide. Secondly, we plan to deploy an automatic calculation formula on the official ClinicalLab website. Users will simply need to input their model's average metric scores for each department to swiftly obtain the DWR. This feature is straightforward to implement on the front-end webpage. We believe these measures will effectively resolve the issues related to the lack of universal applicability of relative metrics. 

Thank you for your suggestion. We will add absolute indicators such as micro-averaged accuracy in the new version to demonstrate the department guidance capabilities of each model.

[1] Using relative and absolute measures for monitoring health inequalities: experiences from cross-national analyses on maternal and child health. Int J Equity Health.

[2] It's Not Your Score That Matters: The Importance of Relative Metrics. 10.4337/9780857938855.00016. 

In Formula CDR, the logic of multiplying the CDR with the metric scores aims to comprehensively evaluate the model's overall performance in complex clinical tasks. Specifically, the CDR evaluates how the model performs in real-world tasks, namely whether it can accurately predict the departmental guide and final diagnosis simultaneously. This serves as a foundational metric to determine if the model is "qualified" at the task level. However, considering only the CDR reflects the frequency of correct decisions made by the model but does not fully capture the quality of the model’s outputs. Metric scores such as BLEU, ROUGE, and BERTScore evaluate the quality of the generated language, reflecting the model’s precision, coherence, and naturalness in expression. Even if the model makes the correct decisions (as indicated by the CDR), inaccurate, incoherent, or unnatural language generation can also affect its effectiveness in practical applications. Thus, evaluating language quality is an important aspect that cannot be overlooked.

Regarding the rationale for multiplying the two metrics: By multiplying the CDR with the metric scores, we ensure that the model is not only accurate in its decisions but also excels in language expression. This product effectively filters out model outputs that perform well both in diagnostic decisions and language quality, rather than models that excel only in one aspect. Thus, the quality of the composite diagnosis and the language quality of the model outputs are both included in the evaluation of overall performance, making the final Acceptability value more comprehensive and accurately reflecting the model’s real-world utility in complex clinical settings. Overall, this logic resembles that of Funnel Analysis.

In summary, multiplying the CDR with metric scores ensures that our chosen model not only makes correct decisions but also produces high-quality language outputs, enabling it to provide effective and reliable support in real-world applications. 

Furthermore, we would like to emphasize that the primary focus of the NeurIPS D&B Track is on the dataset itself. The inclusion of ClinicalMetric serves as a supplementary enhancement rather than a core contribution of our work. We sincerely appreciate your suggestion and will revise the description of “novel metrics” accordingly in future versions. Thank you again for your valuable feedback!


2. Thank you for your recognition of our evaluation methodology and for considering this two-step approach logical. We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s valuable comments on our evaluation framework. We agree that clearly distinguishing between "component-level evaluation" and "end-to-end simulation" is essential for improving the transparency of the paper and accurately conveying the contributions of our work.
Our evaluation framework is designed in two stages:
(1) Component-Level QA Evaluation: In the first stage, we conduct standardized evaluations of 17 LLMs on eight independent clinical tasks using unified inputs and ground-truth answers. This allows us to systematically evaluate each model’s performance in isolation, identify performance gaps, and thereby gain insights to inform the design of ClinicalAgent.
(2) System-Level End-to-End Simulation: In the second stage, we deploy ClinicalAgent in a complete automated clinical simulation workflow. The model is required to perform multi-step reasoning, invoke tools as needed, and integrate and coordinate decisions across multiple tasks, comprehensively simulating real-world clinical scenarios.
We realize that this two-phase evaluation logic was not clearly expressed in the original manuscript. Although the scores for baseline models in Table 2 and Table 4 appear similar (as both come from component-level evaluation), only ClinicalAgent in Table 4 is evaluated under a true end-to-end setting. We will revise the manuscript to elaborate on the motivation behind this two-stage evaluation strategy, and further clarify the distinction between component-level and system-level evaluations through both textual description and visual presentation.
Once again, we thank the reviewer for the constructive suggestions. Your feedback will help us further improve the clarity and academic impact of the paper.

Your insightful comments have been invaluable in refining our paper, and we trust that the clarifications offered above adequately address your concerns. We eagerly await your response to our updated submission and thank you once more for your considerable time and effort.

After thorough discussions with medical professionals, it was concluded that this process is mature and reliable, and no modifications are recommended at this time. 

Regarding your sub-question, "how could the errors in each stage propagate and affect the accuracy in the following stages?" our response is as follows:

Initially, we clearly state in ClinicalAgent’s prompts that the Preliminary Diagnosis (PD) is merely a possible list of diseases, not the final diagnostic outcome. Moreover, in the task design of ClinicalBench, we have ingeniously addressed this potential issue. We require the agent in the Diagnostic Basis (DB) task to find evidence supporting the Preliminary Diagnosis (PD), then proceed with Differential Diagnosis (DD) and Final Diagnosis (FD), until all interfering information is excluded and a final decision is made. This task design mimics the actual diagnostic process of human clinicians: identifying possible diseases, searching for evidence, eliminating one by one, and ultimately making a decision. This design has been discussed multiple times with expert human clinicians and is highly reflective of real-world scenarios, also conforming to the processes recommended in official Chinese medical records (which we have optimized). In other words, throughout the process, ClinicalAgent not only needs to reason but also support its reasoning results with verification. 


2. The clinical evaluation criteria were developed collaboratively with physicians, aiming to cover key decision points in the diagnostic process. We place particular emphasis on department-level triage because an incorrect triage decision can halt the entire diagnostic workflow. Evaluating each department individually reflects real-world practices, as specialists in different departments focus on distinct areas. For example, we believe it is unnecessary for pediatricians to participate in imaging diagnoses; radiologists alone are sufficient for this stage, which closely simulates actual clinical procedures.

3. Our dataset, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols are all publicly available on our GitHub repository, making it easy for others to reproduce our results. The dataset has already been downloaded more than 200 times and has had a broad impact within the community. We would also like to clarify that we did not perform any fine-tuning of models, and we are unsure why the reviewer assumed otherwise.

4. As shown in Table 1, most comparable datasets contain fewer than 1,000 samples. Our dataset includes 1,500 high-quality samples, all of which were annotated through multiple rounds of manual review. As stated in Section 3 of the paper, we are unable to disclose certain details due to hospital regulations that protect patient privacy. This policy aligns with NeurIPS guidelines, and we believe it does not pose a concern for the validity of our research.

5. The data used in this study were obtained from the hospital’s internal database, which is not connected to the internet and complies with strict privacy regulations. We can therefore ensure that there is no risk of data leakage.

summary.value: This work introduces ClinicalLab, a suite designed to fix flaws in medical-AI benchmarks. At its core is ClinicalBench, an end-to-end evaluation benchmark that uses 1,500 real, private clinical cases, thereby preventing the data leakage common in other benchmarks. The authors found that no single LLM excelled across all 24 medical specialties tested. Building on this observation, they created ClinicalAgent, a diagnostic system in which different LLMs, each acting as a “specialist” for a specific department, collaborate on a diagnosis. This collaborative agent significantly outperformed even the best individual LLMs, underscoring the value of aligning AI with real-world medical specialization.

strengths_contributions.value:
- The source dataset of semi-structured patient records, created through a rigorous four-step construction pipeline, is a valuable resource for the research community.
- The benchmark’s main lesson (that no single model performs best across all 24 medical specialties) provides a clear, data-driven rationale that will help researchers design multi-agent clinical diagnosis systems.
- Offering the dataset in both Chinese and English will benefit researchers in both language communities.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The claim of introducing “novel metrics” seems somewhat overstated and could be toned down. While the metrics have new names, their underlying concepts are not new. For instance, the DWR (Department Win Rate) metric is based on a common rank-based scoring system that can be misleading, as it can obscure poor absolute performance across all models. A more meaningful and transparent approach would be to use a standard metric like micro-averaged accuracy. Also, the CDR (Comprehensive Diagnostic Rate) is limited. Despite its name, it does not evaluate the end-to-end diagnostic process comprehensively. Instead, it functions as a simple AND condition on two discrete tasks: the initial department guide and the final diagnosis. This approach completely ignores the quality and correctness of the intermediate clinical reasoning steps. Therefore, it is a restrictive metric that does not fully capture the end-to-end performance it purports to measure, even if some aspects are practical for illustrating model behavior.
- The presentation of the evaluation framework could be clarified to strengthen the paper's claims. While ClinicalBench is introduced as an end-to-end benchmark, the initial evaluation of the 17 LLMs is conducted on eight separate tasks, each provided with ground-truth inputs. This makes this first phase of evaluation function more as a collection of QA benchmarks rather than a test of sequential decision-making. Furthermore, this leads to a difference in evaluation mechanisms when comparing the baseline LLMs to ClinicalAgent. As the scores for the baseline LLMs are identical in Table 2 and Table 4, it is clear that only ClinicalAgent undergoes a true end-to-end simulation, while the baselines are represented by their component-level scores. Although this two-step methodology is logical (first analyzing components to inform the design of a superior system and then testing that system holistically), the paper would benefit from explicitly detailing this rationale. A clearer distinction between the 'component-level QA evaluation' and the 'system-level end-to-end simulation' would make the significant performance leap of ClinicalAgent even more impactful and transparent to readers.

dataset_code_comments.value: Accessibility is limited due to a gated access model and a highly restrictive license. Access requires submitting a Google Form and agreeing to terms that strictly prohibit using the dataset for training models, creating derivative works, or redistribution.

final_justification.value: The authors addressed my concerns by adding baseline end-to-end evaluations and introducing improved evaluation metrics, such as micro-averaged accuracy. The remaining concern is ensuring these improvements are clearly integrated into the revised manuscript, as the original version did not sufficiently benefit from such content. I will raise my score to "Borderline Accept".

summary.value:
This paper introduces ClinicalLab for clinical diagnosis agent alignment. The work consists of three main components:
- ClinicalBench: An end-to-end multi-departmental clinical diagnostic evaluation benchmark based on real cases covering 24 departments and 150 diseases across 1500 samples.
- ClinicalMetrics: Four evaluation metrics (Department Win Rate, Department Instruction Following Rate, Comprehensive Diagnostic Rate, and Acceptability) designed to measure LLM effectiveness in clinical scenarios.
- ClinicalAgent: A multi-agent clinical diagnostic system that dynamically allocates specialists from different departments based on patient complaints.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The benchmark design closely mimics real clinical workflows, enhancing real-world applicability. It has good coverage: 24 departments and 150 diseases provide comprehensive medical scope.
2. The proposed ClinicalMetrics provides a multi-dimensional view of agent performance, addressing limitations of existing multiple-choice evaluation approaches.
3. The proposed multi-agent approach is intuitive and mirrors actual medical practice.
4. The data curation and model evaluation appseemsears rigorous. Detailed procedures are described in the manuscript.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. Although performance across departments is reported, the paper does not investigate whether certain LLMs display systematic biases or failure modes for specific demographics, disease severity levels, or rare conditions.
2. The benchmark is primarily Chinese-based, with only machine-translated English samples for optional use. No evaluation of the translation quality was provided. This might limit its accessibility and global impact.
3. The evaluation relies on BLEU, ROUGE, and BertScore metrics. Despite authors' efforts in minimizing errors due to synonym variations and ensuring the accuracy of the metrics, these metrics may not fully capture the correctness and clinical appropriateness of medical reasoning, as they primarily measure surface-level text similarity rather than semantic accuracy or clinical validity.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: Code is partially available (no evaluation). Dataset is applied for access.

final_justification.value: I'll keep my rating of 5. While I agree with other reviewers that the manuscript has some flaw in experiments and evaluation, I think the dataset itself can benefit the community.

summary.value: The paper introduces ClinicalLab, a comprehensive framework for evaluating and aligning clinical diagnostic agents powered by large language models (LLMs). ClinicalLab consists of three key components: ClinicalBench, ClinicalMetrics, and ClinicalAgent. ClinicalBench is a multi-departmental, end-to-end benchmark built from real clinical case data spanning 24 departments and 150 diseases. It is designed to assess LLMs in realistic diagnostic scenarios beyond traditional multiple-choice settings. ClinicalMetrics is a suite of four custom evaluation metrics (CDR, DIFR, DWR, Acceptability) intended to capture diagnostic correctness and alignment with clinical practices. ClinicalAgent is an end-to-end clinical diagnostic agent that performs a six-stage diagnostic process, meant to reflect how real-world clinical workflows operate. The authors benchmark 17 general and medical-domain LLMs (e.g., GPT-4, MetaMed, InternLM) on ClinicalBench and demonstrate that ClinicalAgent outperforms them in end-to-end diagnostic performance. The paper emphasizes real-world alignment, robustness, and ethical considerations in medical AI evaluation.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper addresses a critical need for robust evaluation frameworks for clinical diagnostic agents using large language models (LLMs), aligning with growing interest in AI for healthcare.

2. ClinicalBench covers 24 medical departments and 150 diseases, providing broad task diversity across specialties.

3. The benchmark is built from real clinical case data (albeit private), making it more reflective of real-world diagnostic complexity than synthetic or MCQ-based datasets.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. While the paper claims that ClinicalBench supports end-to-end evaluation, in practice, LLMs are assessed on isolated tasks using ground-truth inputs, rather than through sequential, interactive decision-making as a real agent would operate. If some intermediate steps in the diagnostic process yield accuracies as low as 20–30% (as shown in Table 2), what are the implications for the final diagnosis or treatment plan—the true end-to-end objective? The paper does not discuss whether such low accuracy propagates through the diagnostic chain, nor whether error accumulation undermines the overall outcome. It also remains unclear whether it is optimal for LLMs to follow a six-stage diagnostic process sequentially, or if directly predicting the final treatment plan would yield better results. While intermediate reasoning steps may benefit human clinicians, LLMs may not derive the same utility. Ablation studies and deeper analysis are necessary to justify the chosen approach. This fatal flaw is at the core of this benchmark and needs to be fixed immediately. 

2. ClinicalMetrics (CDR, DWR, DIFR) either repurpose or slightly modify existing evaluation techniques, lacking substantial novelty. DIFR is more aligned with instruction-following rather than clinical reasoning. CDR combines department guide and disease diagnosis, but the rationale for this design choice is unclear. Is this suggesting that only the error in department guide affects the diagnosis, and the differential diagnosis, etc., do not affect the final diagnosis? This reiterates the problem with the first weakness that there is no metric to reflect the final error accumulated through the six sequential stages. Moreover, the metrics evaluate each department separately, rather than considering the cases that involves cross-departmental collaboration. The example in your Figure 1 clearly states imageological examination, which is conducted by an individual department.

3. There is not sufficient information for reproducibility. There are no sufficient details in data preprocessing, prompt formulation, model fine-tuning, hyperparameters, and evaluation protocols, which are all key elements necessary to replicate results. The generative QA component is also insufficiently described. 

4. The dataset contains only 1,500 samples, which is too small. Moreover, the paper does not provide demographic breakdowns (e.g., age, sex, comorbidity distribution), making it difficult to assess generalizability or fairness. There is minimal discussion on potential biases in the dataset or model performance across demographic subgroups (e.g., sex, age, race), which is critical for clinical AI applications.

5. Although the paper claims the dataset is free of data leakage, no methodological explanation or validation process is provided to substantiate that claim.

6. The paper mentions using 8 A6000 GPUs and API calls but does not report compute costs (training time, inference time, FLOPs, etc.) or comparisons with resource requirements for other benchmarks.

7. The names of certain models are vague. For example, what exact model in what exact release date is used for Claude 3, Gemini?

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The data access requires one to fill out a form. This is not strictly open source by standard definitions. That's typically closer to a "shared upon request" model. In contrast, most machine learning and systems papers released at conferences expect fully open access, meaning anyone can clone or download the dataset and code directly (e.g., from a public repository) without gating.

additional_feedback.value: In general, this could have been a good contribution by releasing new dataset, small as it is. However, the issues with no statistical summary about the data, restricted access to data, no sufficient details on benchmarking, problems in evaluation are the key barriers for me to recommend the paper for acceptance. If these can be resolved, I am more than glad to raise my score to very high. But at this moment, this paper is not ready yet for publication in a rigorous and prestigious venue (NeurIPS, JAMIA, etc.).

final_justification.value: The rebuttal has been helpful in at least making more clarity on the eval pipeline. Love to see the full comprehensive eval promised by the authors.

title.value: ClinicalLab: Aligning Agents for Multi-Departmental Clinical Diagnostics in the Real World

abstract.value: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved significant performance progress in various natural language processing applications. However, LLMs still struggle to meet the strict requirements for accuracy and reliability in the medical field and face many challenges in clinical applications. Existing clinical diagnostic evaluation benchmarks for evaluating medical agents powered by LLMs have severe limitations. To address these limitations, we introduce ClinicalLab, a comprehensive clinical diagnosis agent alignment suite. ClinicalLab includes ClinicalBench, an end-to-end multi-departmental clinical diagnostic evaluation benchmark for evaluating medical agents and LLMs. ClinicalBench is based on real cases that cover 24 departments and 150 diseases. We ensure that ClinicalBench does not have data leakage. ClinicalLab also includes four novel metrics (ClinicalMetrics) for evaluating the effectiveness of LLMs in clinical diagnostic tasks. We evaluate 17 general and medical-domain LLMs and find that their performance varies significantly across different departments. Based on these findings, in ClinicalLab, we propose ClinicalAgent, an end-to-end clinical agent that aligns with real-world clinical diagnostic practices. We systematically investigate the performance and applicable scenarios of variants of ClinicalAgent on ClinicalBench. Our findings demonstrate the importance of aligning with modern medical practices in designing medical agents.

croissant_file.description: If you checked the Dataset Submission box, upload a Croissant metadata file that documents your dataset. dataset_final_confirmation.description: **By checking this box, you confirm that: (1)** your dataset is complete and finalized at the time of submission; **(2)** you included a valid Croissant metadata file that has been verified using the [Croissant validator](https://huggingface.co/spaces/luisoala/croissant-checker); **(3)** you followed the [NeurIPS2025 data hosting guidelines](https://neurips.cc/Conferences/2025/DataHostingGuidelines); **(4)** you provided a URL pointing to the dataset that is accessible for NeurIPS2025 reviewers. If you left the Dataset Submission box unchecked, leave this box unchecked.

checklist_confirmation.description: In order to improve the rigor and transparency of research submitted to and published at NeurIPS, authors are required to complete a paper checklist and include it in the paper PDF. supplementary_material.description: All supplementary material must be self-contained and zipped into a single file. Note that supplementary material will be visible to reviewers throughout and after the review period, and **ensure all your supplementary material is anonymized if your submission is anonymized.** The maximum file size is 100MB. Supplementary material can be updated until the supplementary material deadline (May 22).

financial_support.description: Optionally indicate one student author on the paper who would need financial support to attend and present at the conference if the paper is accepted (or leave blank if financial support is not needed). Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors.

reviewer_nomination.description: Every submission must nominate at least one author who is a qualified reviewer (i.e., satisfying our reviewer nomination criteria [https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/](https://blog.neurips.cc/2025/03/10/self-nomination-for-reviewing-at-neurips-2025/) ). Being named as such a reviewer in the submission constitutes an acceptance and a commitment to carry out the regular reviewing load (~6 papers) responsibly if asked by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. Only if no qualified reviewer exists in the author list, nominate the best-qualified author for consideration by the PC chairs or the D&B track chairs. In addition, note that any author listed on 4 or more papers will be automatically regarded as a reviewer unless they are already serving as a reviewer, AC, SAC, or other roles in the Organization Committee. Failure to assign a qualified reviewer when one is available in the author list may result in desk rejection. Please enter an email address or an OpenReview ID that exactly matches one of the authors (separate by comma if more than one nominations).

responsible_reviewing.description: We acknowledge that every author on the program committee is obligated to conduct responsible reviewing according to the policy designed by the PC Chairs and relevant members of the organizing committee. **Failure to do so may result in desk rejection or other serious consequences.**
